docs.title: OpenAPI Petstore
docs.text:
The OpenAPI Petstore is the standard Swagger/OpenAPI sample API (OpenAPI 3.1.0) with a working server, petstore-server, that serves every operation from memory. The server can also act as an AAuth resource: each operation asks an AI agent for exactly the trust it needs, from just its identity to the person's approval of a scope.

That makes it a small, realistic target for testing agents and AAuth implementations against each other.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
• Test AAuth interop runs the Petstore next to the AAuth sandbox and checks an agent, a person server or your own implementation against it.
  • Postman AI readiness scores how usable the API is by an AI agent, with the Postman CLI.
  • The README covers running the server, its flags and the container image.

docs.title: The Spec
docs.text: The spec, openapi.yaml, is at the repository root. The server embeds it and serves it at /openapi.yaml and /openapi.json. Each operation's x-aauth annotation says what it requires in AAuth mode. The Postman smoke collection and mock are under postman/.

docs.title: Test AAuth Interop
docs.text: Use the Petstore as an AAuth resource to check that an agent, a person server or an agent provider of your own works with the others. The servers around it come from the AAuth sandbox in aauth-go, which has the full sandbox guide; this page covers what is specific to the Petstore.

docs.title: What Each Operation Asks For
docs.text:
In AAuth mode (--auth aauth) each operation requires what its x-aauth annotation in openapi.yaml says, so one resource exercises every level:

Level Operations An agent must Agent identity findPetsByStatus, findPetsByTags, getPetById, getInventory, loginUser, logoutUser sign the request with its agent token Person getOrderById, the user operations present a person token Auth token, write:orders placeOrder, deleteOrder get the person's approval, then present the auth token Auth token, write:pets addPet, updatePet, updatePetWithForm, deletePet, uploadFile the same, for write:pets

Orders belong to the person who placed them: another person's order is not found. The resource metadata, with the scope descriptions a person server shows on its consent page, is at /.well-known/aauth-resource.json.

docs.title: Run It with the Sandbox
docs.text:
The aauth-postman repository has a Compose file that runs the sandbox and the Petstore together, with the Petstore fronted at https://petstore.aauth.test:

cd aauth-postman
docker compose --profile petstore up -d --build --wait
docker compose --profile petstore run --rm newman-petstore   # a reference agent

The base sandbox starts without the petstore profile; the profile adds the Petstore as a resource server of its own, behind the sandbox.

The Compose file builds the Petstore image from this repository, found at ../../grokify/petstore unless you set PETSTORE_DIR. To run the pieces by hand, see the flags in the README.

docs.title: Check Your Agent
docs.text:
Enroll at the sandbox's agent provider, then call the Petstore. A correct agent sees these responses, in order:

  1. GET /v2/pet/findByStatus?status=available signed with the agent token: 200.
  2. POST /v2/store/order: 401, AAuth-Requirement: requirement=person-token.
  3. The same request with a person token: 401, requirement=auth-token, with a resource token for write:orders.
  4. The resource token sent to the person server's token endpoint: 202 with an interaction code while the person approves, then 200 with the auth token.
  5. The order repeated with the auth token: 200.

The sandbox records every message:

docker compose exec sandbox aauth-sandbox trace --state /state

Two reference agents send these messages. The Postman collection shows each as one request, and omniagent is an AI agent that does the whole exchange itself. Comparing your agent's trace with theirs shows where it differs.

docs.title: Check Your Own Server Instead
docs.text: To test a person server or agent provider of your own, start the sandbox with --remote (Test another implementation) and run the same agent against the Petstore. The Petstore trusts the person server named by --trust, so give it your server's origin.

docs.title: Reset the Store
docs.text:
The store is in memory and starts with six pets. A pet that an order sells is gone until the server restarts:

docker compose --profile petstore up -d --force-recreate petstore

docs.title: MySQL Tools
docs.text: create_tables and create_pets create the Petstore pet table in a MySQL database and measure inserts. main.java is a JBang example that connects to the same databases from Java. BenchmarkPet in the models package inserts pets the same way as a Go benchmark.

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text:
The tools read the databases they can use from a JSON file, named by the PETSTORE_DATASOURCES environment variable. It maps a name to a data source; the repository carries an example, models/cmd/datasources.example.json:

{
  "MY8MICRO": {
    "driver": "mysql",
    "hostname": "db.example.com",
    "port": 3306,
    "user": "testuser",
    "password": "your-password",
    "database": "petstore"
  }
}

The file holds credentials, so keep it outside the repository, for example at ~/.config/petstore/datasources.json, and restrict it with chmod 600. The tools refuse a file that other users can read. Windows does not enforce file modes, so the check is skipped there.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
export PETSTORE_DATASOURCES=~/.config/petstore/datasources.json
go run ./models/cmd/create_tables -t MY8MICRO
go run ./models/cmd/create_pets -t MY8MICRO -i 1000

If the name is not in the file, the tools list the names it holds. create_pets prints the host, the server version and the row count before it inserts, then the elapsed time. create_tables prints only the database and host, never the password.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
BenchmarkPet needs a second variable for the entry to use, and is skipped without it:

PETSTORE_BENCH_DATASOURCE=MY8MICRO go test ./models -bench Pet -benchtime 1000x

docs.title: Java Example
docs.text:
models/cmd/create_pets/main.java connects with the MySQL Connector/J 5.1 driver over TLS 1.2, which MySQL 5.7 servers accept. It takes the connection details and the number of inserts as arguments:

jbang models/cmd/create_pets/main.java <host> <port> <database> <user> <password> <iterations>

The password is a command-line argument here, so other users on the machine can see it in the process list. Use a throwaway database.

docs.title: Run the Server
docs.text: petstore-server serves every operation in the Petstore OpenAPI definition (openapi.yaml, OpenAPI 3.1) from memory. It can also act as an AAuth resource, so each operation asks an AI agent for exactly the trust it needs.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text:
go run ./cmd/petstore-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8080
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/v2/pet/findByStatus?status=available'
  • Operations. All 20 operations of the spec are routed under the spec's base path, /v2: the pet, store and user groups.
  • Store. It starts with six pets and keeps everything in memory, so a pet that an order sells is gone, and anything you add is lost, when the server restarts.
  • Spec. The spec is served at /openapi.yaml and /openapi.json, with servers pointing at the server, so tools that load an OpenAPI document find it there. The server embeds the spec; it is also importable as the Go package github.com/grokify/petstore.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Flag Meaning --listen the address to listen on, plain HTTP (default :8080); put TLS in front, as the sandbox does --auth none (default) serves every operation to anyone; aauth makes the server an AAuth resource --url the resource's public URL and AAuth identifier, such as https://petstore.aauth.test --trust a person server whose tokens to accept (repeatable; required with --auth aauth) --ca-file a PEM file of an extra root CA for fetching issuers' keys, such as the sandbox CA

docs.title: Run It as an AAuth Resource
docs.text:
With --auth aauth, each operation requires what its x-aauth annotation in openapi.yaml says, from the agent's identity up to the person's approval of a scope. The levels, and how to run the server next to the AAuth sandbox and check an agent against it, are in Test AAuth interop.

The resource metadata is at /.well-known/aauth-resource.json, with the scope descriptions a person server shows on its consent page.

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
docker build -t petstore-server .
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 petstore-server

The image is static and runs as a non-root user. It has no shell or curl, so its health check is the server's own health subcommand, which asks a running server for its spec:

petstore-server health --addr 127.0.0.1:8080

Publish the port on 127.0.0.1 as above unless you mean to expose an unauthenticated server: without --auth aauth anyone who can reach it can change its pets.

docs.title: Postman — AI Readiness Report
docs.text:
Scored with postman spec ai-readiness ./openapi.yaml (Postman CLI 1.60.0) against the git-registered spec (inputType: FILE_PATH).

:material-file-chart: Open full HTML report :material-code-json: Download JSON

docs.title: Headline
docs.text:
Metric Value Readiness 80 / 100 — Excellent Confidence high (0 signals unknown) Doc coverage high (adjustment −1) Complexity 2 / 10 — Simple Endpoints 20 Schemas 6

Why the score moved from 90 to 80 after we improved the spec

We documented credential acquisition, added response examples, and exposed rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit-*). That resolved both previously-unknown signals, so confidence rose from medium to high. But the readiness score fell 90 → 80: the rubric folds rate limiting into complexity (rate_limiting: complex, complexity 1→2/10), and readiness tracks inversely. In other words, better documentation made the API's real complexity visible — the score didn't get worse, our measurement of it got honest.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Addressed in the spec: ✅ credential acquisition documented · ✅ response examples added · ✅ rate limiting exposed. Remaining, and largely inherent to the API's shape:

  • Scope the surface. 20 endpoints is large; point an agent at a focused subset, or split the spec into smaller domains.
  • Simplify parameters. Reduce parameter count or document each parameter's role — agents select parameters from descriptions.

docs.title: Full report
docs.text:
The command's own HTML report is served as a static asset and embedded below (passthrough rendering).

Prefer a standalone tab? Open the report directly.

docs.title: Release Notes - v0.1.0
docs.text:
Release Date: 2023-09-04

v0.1.0 is the first release. It defines the Petstore pet table for MySQL and adds two small commands that create the table and measure how fast pets can be inserted, along with a Java example that does the same over JDBC.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Pet Table - The Petstore pet table, as a SQL definition and as a Go function, models.CreatePetTable, that creates it in a MySQL database.
  • Table and Insert Tools - create_tables creates the table in a named database, and create_pets inserts pets and reports how long they took, so the same workload can be compared across MySQL versions and instance sizes.
  • Java Example - A JBang script inserts pets through JDBC, for comparing a Java client with the Go one.

docs.title: The Table
docs.text: models/create_pet.sql defines the pet table: an auto-increment id, a name, a description, a status, acquisition and birth dates and times, creation and update times, and a category_id. The SQL is embedded in the models package, and CreatePetTable(db) runs it.

docs.title: The Commands
docs.text:
go run ./models/cmd/create_tables -t <environment>
go run ./models/cmd/create_pets -t <environment> -i 1000

-t names the database to use, and -i is the number of pets to insert (10 by default). create_pets prints the host, the server version, the row count, the elapsed time and the duration in minutes.

docs.title: The Java Example
docs.text: models/cmd/create_pets/main.java connects with JDBC and inserts pets, reporting the same timings.

docs.title: Full Changelog
docs.text: See CHANGELOG.md for the complete list of changes.

docs.title: Release Notes - v0.2.0
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-26

v0.2.0 turns the Petstore from a table definition into a running API. petstore-server serves every operation of the Swagger Petstore from memory, and it can act as an AAuth resource, so an AI agent has a realistic API that asks for different levels of trust. The release also adds a container image, a documentation site, and makes the MySQL tools build from a clean clone.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Petstore Server - petstore-server serves the 20 operations of the Petstore OpenAPI 3.1 definition from memory, seeded with six pets, and serves the spec at /openapi.yaml and /openapi.json.
  • AAuth Resource Mode - With --auth aauth, each operation requires the access its x-aauth annotation names: the agent's identity, the person, or an auth token for write:orders or write:pets. Orders belong to the person who placed them.
  • Spec as a Go Package - The OpenAPI definition is embedded in package petstore, with an x-aauth annotation on every operation.
  • Container Image - A static, non-root image runs the server, with a health subcommand for health checks in a shell-less image.
  • Clean-Clone MySQL Tools - create_tables, create_pets and the benchmark read their databases from a private JSON file, so the repository builds without any file that was left out of it.

docs.title: The Server
docs.text:
go run ./cmd/petstore-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8080
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/v2/pet/findByStatus?status=available'
Flag Meaning --listen the address to listen on, plain HTTP (default :8080) --auth none (default) or aauth --url the resource's public URL and AAuth identifier --trust a person server whose tokens to accept (repeatable) --ca-file an extra root CA for fetching issuers' keys, such as the sandbox CA

The store lives in memory, so a restart brings back the six seeded pets. See the Run the Server guide.

docs.title: AAuth
docs.text: In AAuth mode the server accepts person and auth tokens only from the person servers you give with --trust, and publishes its resource metadata and scope descriptions at /.well-known/aauth-resource.json. Run it behind the aauth-go sandbox and check an agent against it with the interop guide. The tests cover every operation and run the server behind the aauth-go sandbox as an enrolled agent.

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
docker build -t petstore-server .
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 petstore-server

Publish the port on 127.0.0.1 unless you mean to expose a server that, without --auth aauth, lets anyone change its pets.

docs.title: MySQL tools
docs.text:
The tools no longer carry database hostnames or credentials in source. They read them from the JSON file that PETSTORE_DATASOURCES names:

  • Create the file from models/cmd/datasources.example.json, keep it outside the repository, and run chmod 600 on it. The tools refuse a file that other users can read.
  • cmd.GetDataSourceSet() is replaced by cmd.LoadDataSourceSet(), which returns an error. Go code that called the old function must handle it.
  • create_tables prints the database and host, no longer the whole data source with its password.
  • BenchmarkPet is skipped unless PETSTORE_BENCH_DATASOURCE names an entry of that file.

See the MySQL Tools guide.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: The module requires aauth-go v0.3.0 and mogo v0.75.0, and its go directive is now 1.27.0, where v0.1.0 needed Go 1.20. Update your toolchain before building from source.

docs.title: PLAN — Petstore server with optional AAuth
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-PETSTORE-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/petstore

  1. Annotate the spec with x-aauth and scope descriptions.
  2. Build the store and the handlers for all operations, then the spec-driven router, with tests that every operation is routed.
  3. Add AAuth mode with aauth-go's ResourceGuard, tested end to end with aauth-go's Transport against an in-process person server.
  4. Add the petstore-server command, the image, and the guide.

The server depends on aauth-go v0.3.0.

docs.title: PRD — Petstore server with optional AAuth
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PETSTORE-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/petstore

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The Swagger Petstore is the API most developers already know, and this repository carries its OpenAPI definition, but no server. Demos of agent authorization need a resource that an agent can call for real: one with operations that need different levels of trust, and a spec an agent can load as a tool set.

AAuth (draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol) lets a resource ask for exactly what each operation needs: the agent's identity, the person the agent acts for, or the person's consent for a scope. The Postman collection and the omniagent demo should call the same resource, behind the same person server and agent provider, so the two demos mirror each other.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• petstore-server serves every operation in openapi.yaml from memory, seeded with pets, with no database.
  • With --auth aauth it is an AAuth resource: each operation's access level comes from an x-aauth annotation in the spec, so the spec documents the policy the server enforces.
  • Without it, it is a plain Petstore, for API demos that do not involve AAuth.
  • It runs behind the aauth-go sandbox as https://petstore.aauth.test, and as a container.
  • It serves its own spec, with servers pointing at itself, for agents that load an OpenAPI document as tools.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• XML responses, real image storage, or persistence across restarts.
  • The legacy api_key and OAuth security schemes: the spec keeps them for reference, the server does not enforce them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Access levels. Reads of the catalog need the agent's identity. Orders and user accounts need the person. Changing the catalog needs an auth token for write:pets, and placing or cancelling an order an auth token for write:orders, so the person approves each.
  2. Per-person data. Orders belong to the person who placed them, keyed by the person's issuer and subject. A person cannot read another's order.
  3. Trust. The server accepts person and auth tokens only from the person servers named with --trust.
  4. Spec-driven routes. Every operation in the spec has a handler and an x-aauth annotation; the server refuses to start otherwise.

docs.title: TRD — Petstore server with optional AAuth
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PETSTORE-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/petstore

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Contents petstore.go Package petstore: the embedded openapi.yaml server/ Package server: store, handlers, spec-driven router cmd/petstore-server/ Cobra command over server

docs.title: Spec annotations
docs.text:
Each operation carries x-aauth:

x-aauth:
  access: auth        # agent | person | auth
  scope: write:pets   # required when access is auth

The top level carries x-aauth.scopes, the descriptions published as the resource metadata's scope_descriptions for consent screens.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
server.New reads the spec's operations (method, path, operationId, x-aauth) and the base path of its first server URL (/v2). It registers each operation on an http.ServeMux as METHOD /v2/path; OpenAPI path templates ({petId}) are ServeMux wildcards. With a guard, each handler is wrapped by ResourceGuard.Require (aauth-go), and the guard's WellKnown handler serves /.well-known/aauth-resource.json and /jwks.json.

GET /openapi.yaml and GET /openapi.json serve the spec with servers replaced by the server's public URL and base path.

docs.title: AAuth mode
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --auth aauth enable AAuth --url the resource's identifier, such as https://petstore.aauth.test --trust person server issuers to accept (repeatable) --ca-file extra root CA for fetching issuers' keys (the sandbox CA)

The resource signing key is generated at start; its public key is served at /jwks.json, so restarts need no key file.

docs.title: Store
docs.text: A mutex-guarded in-memory store: pets by ID, orders by ID with the owner's (iss, sub), users by username. Passwords are accepted and never returned.
